blocks.text: …if it has to be reliable
The “down” procedure is suitable for all situations in which the dog is exposed to strong distraction which, however, does not present itself as problematic in the sense of pressing the dog.
“Down” is the ultimate means of choice for reliably keeping our dog from hunting, rummaging, running away and other unwanted actions, or interrupting it in them.

A well-trained “down” allows us to lay our dog down in one place, independent of distraction, even over a longer period of time. Beyond that, it is an elegant way to relax encounter situations between dogs.
The prerequisite for all “down” scenarios is, of course, smooth execution.
Start, prerequisites & training frequency 📅
Start: From about the 5th to 6th month of age.
Training frequency: At first, in a distraction-free environment, 5 to 10 separate exercises daily – not carried out consecutively.
Over the next weeks and months, the exercise frequency increases to 20 to 30 “down” applications, each with a different duration and gradually increasing external distraction.
“Down” must be trained and requested in the widest variety of places. The success of this exercise depends on repetition, variety and calm composure.
Execution & training environment 🐕
Ideally we train “down” during the walk while on the leash: address the dog by name to establish attention, walk a few steps sideways – later rather backwards – and calmly say “down”.
The melody of the word “down” should be calm, carrying and falling towards the end. “Down” should by no means be pronounced in a high voice with raised intonation.

The dog should turn towards us in the movement and is then moved into the down with a hand signal (the flat hand moves downwards) and support from a flowing pull on the harness or collar. By no means should it be pressed down from above on the shoulders or back.
Note on food & showing 💡
“Down” training exclusively by means of food or only by showing is possible, but experience shows it to be unreliable in real situations with high distraction.
In case of doubt there is then no longer any possibility to interrupt and secure our dog in the event of danger.
Remember: “Down” is a must-do exercise, not a can-do exercise.
Step 1: Attention & positioning 👁️
During the walk on the leash, address the dog by its name and thereby establish attention.
At the same time walk a few steps sideways and calmly say “down” with falling intonation.
Step 2: Hand signal & leash support ✋
Accompany the dog into the down with the flat hand moving downwards and a flowing pull on the harness or collar.
No pressure from above on shoulders or back. No hard tightening of the leash.
Step 3: Duration & calm ⏳
At the beginning it is sufficient for our dog to stay down for several seconds without further help.
Praise is given only after the “down” has been released – not while the dog is lying, since early praise destabilises the position.
Step 4: Release with “sit” 🔄
The procedure is ended by a motivatingly spoken “sit”, followed by vigorous praise.
The dog is not pulled upwards in doing so. We call it affectionately by its name, go back 2 steps, and as soon as it gets up, we calmly say “sit”.
Step 5: Further development – duration & distance 🎯

Over the course of the weeks, in individual exercises we extend the duration of lying down to several minutes and also leave the lying dog in terms of location – but always only as far as that we can quickly be at the dog if it gets up prematurely.

In this case we absolutely put it back in its original place. As an exception, a slightly different place may be chosen if the original place no longer allows it – for example because of a sudden change in conditions (dangers, insects, pressure).
By no means force the dog back into the down if there are recognisable obstacles or the dog shows stress reactions.

Calling the dog out of the “down” position over a distance is only recommended once “down” is consolidated to the point that our dog no longer leaves the position under strong distraction. Until then, collecting it on the spot is more effective and preserves the reliability of the exercise.
What you should avoid ⚠️
Avoid sharply spoken commands in training and in everyday use.
Avoid keeping the leash short or – as is still taught in some places – putting your foot on the leash.
Bringing the dog into the down by stepping on the leash or by so-called submission gestures is to be regarded as wrong and destructive and is therefore to be avoided in principle.
Avoid a down turned away from the handler.
Avoid early praise during the down procedure.
Avoid stress during the exercise.
Avoid the dog leaving the down on its own.
Practical impulse: Variety as the key

Consciously train “down” in different places – in front of the supermarket, at the edge of the woods, in the car park. Every new place is a new test and strengthens reliability. The dog learns: “down” applies everywhere, not just at home on the carpet.
→ Did I make sure of a calm and distraction-free environment?
→ Did I carry out the training daily and repeatedly?
→ Did I change the training locations?
→ Did I always walk sideways or backwards for support?
→ Did I observe calm communication with the dog?
→ Did I support with hand signal and leash aid?
→ Did I leave the dog lying until it had settled?
→ Was every down properly concluded with “sit”?
→ Did I praise calmly and intensively?
